overview:
Suriname is the smallest country in South America, tucked on the northeast shoulder of the continent between Guyana and French Guiana, with Brazil to the south and the Atlantic Ocean to the north. It covers about 164,000 km², similar to Florida, and rainforest blankets more than 90 percent of it, one of the highest proportions of any country.

Only about 620,000 people live here, nearly all of them on the narrow coastal plain. Dutch is the official language, a reminder of colonial rule, while Sranan Tongo, an English-based creole, is the everyday shared tongue, and Hindi, Javanese, Chinese and Indigenous languages are also spoken. Paramaribo, the capital, has a historic center of white wooden Dutch buildings beside the Suriname River.

Suriname is a presidential republic. Gold, oil and bauxite drive its economy, and offshore oil discoveries could change it considerably.
landAndNature: Behind the muddy coastal strip and its mangroves rise savannas and then a huge, almost roadless interior of tropical forest, cut by black-water rivers and rapids. The Central Suriname Nature Reserve protects an area larger than some countries, including the Voltzberg, a bare granite dome that pushes above the canopy. The Brokopondo reservoir, made by damming the Suriname River in the 1960s, flooded a vast area and left drowned trees standing in the water. Jaguars, giant river otters, tapirs, harpy eagles and eight kinds of monkey live in the forest, and the Guiana cock-of-the-rock, a flame-orange bird, displays on rocky slopes. Leatherback turtles, the largest turtles on Earth, nest on the beaches at Galibi.
peopleAndCulture: Suriname is one of the most diverse countries anywhere: descendants of Indian and Javanese indentured workers, Africans brought in slavery, Chinese and Dutch settlers, Lebanese traders, and Indigenous Kalina and Lokono peoples live side by side. Mosques stand beside synagogues and Hindu temples in Paramaribo. Maroon communities, descended from Africans who escaped plantations and built free societies in the forest, keep distinct languages, drumming and wood carving, and still govern their own villages. Food reflects everything at once: Indian roti, Javanese bami and saoto soup, Chinese noodles, and pom, a baked dish of grated root vegetable and chicken served at every celebration. Soccer is the leading sport, and many Dutch stars have Surinamese roots.
history: Indigenous peoples lived along the rivers long before Europeans arrived. The English settled here briefly, then in 1667 traded the colony to the Dutch in exchange for New Amsterdam, which became New York. The Dutch built sugar, coffee and cotton plantations worked by enslaved Africans under brutal conditions; many escaped into the interior and formed Maroon communities that fought the colonists and won treaties recognizing their freedom in the 1760s. Slavery was abolished in 1863, and planters then recruited indentured laborers from India and Java, which is why the country is so mixed today. Suriname became independent from the Netherlands on November 25, 1975, and about a third of the population moved to the Netherlands around that time. Military rule in the 1980s gave way to elected government.
funFacts: The Dutch swapped New York for Suriname in 1667, trading Manhattan to England for a sugar colony.
More than 90 percent of Suriname is covered in forest, making it one of the greenest countries on Earth.
Paramaribo's main square has a mosque and a synagogue standing peacefully next door to each other.
Maroon peoples in the interior descend from Africans who escaped plantations and won their freedom by treaty in the 1700s.
Suriname is the only country in the Americas where Dutch is the official language.
